title: Facade and Flyweight
scopeHtml: Scope: Facade over subsystems, Flyweight intrinsic/extrinsic state, before/after refactors, when not to use, MediaPlayer, Integer cache, Glide pools. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Facade: the idea
notes.html:
A Facade gives one simple front door to a complicated subsystem. Clients call one easy method; the facade orchestrates the many classes behind it. It does not stop you using the subsystem directly if you really need to.

Mechanism: a class that holds references to several subsystem objects and exposes a few coarse-grained methods that call them in the right order.

+----------+      +------------------+       +--------------+
| Client   | ---> | OrderFacade      | ----> | Inventory    |
+----------+      | + placeOrder()   | ----> | Payment      |
                  +------------------+ ----> | Shipping     |
                                       ----> | Notification |

Worked example. Placing an order needs: reserve stock (1 call), charge card (1 call), create shipment (1 call), send email (1 call). Without a facade each of 12 screens repeats those 4 calls and their error handling: 48 call sites. With a facade there are 4 calls in 1 place plus 12 one-line callers.

Industry examples. Android MediaPlayer hides decoders, buffers and audio output behind start()/pause(). Retrofit's Retrofit.create() front door. SLF4J LoggerFactory. Spring's JdbcTemplate is a facade over JDBC connection, statement, result set and cleanup. Stripe's PaymentIntent API is a facade over card networks, 3DS and fraud checks.

Everyday analogy. A hotel concierge: you say "dinner for two at 8" and they handle the phone calls, booking and the taxi.

Decision gravity. Easy to add and reversible; the facade's method signatures become a public contract. Moving a transaction boundary inside it later (all-or-nothing vs best-effort) is behavior-changing, so decide consistency rules up front.

Common interview traps.

  • Facade vs Adapter: Facade simplifies MANY classes into a new simple interface; Adapter converts ONE interface into an existing expected one.
  • Letting the facade become a god class holding all business logic.

notes.title: Facade in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before.

// BEFORE: every caller knows the order and the failure handling
inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
try {
    payment.charge(card, amount);
} catch (PaymentException e) {
    inventory.release(sku, qty);   // easy to forget
    throw e;
}
shipping.create(address, sku);
email.send(user, "Order placed");

After.

class OrderFacade {
    private final Inventory inventory; private final Payment payment;
    private final Shipping shipping;   private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderFacade(Inventory i, Payment p, Shipping s, Notifier n) {
        inventory = i; payment = p; shipping = s; notifier = n;
    }
    public void placeOrder(String user, String sku, int qty, double amount) {
        inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
        try {
            payment.charge(user, amount);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            inventory.release(sku, qty);   // compensation lives in one place
            throw e;
        }
        shipping.create(user, sku);
        notifier.send(user, "Order placed");
    }
}
// facade.placeOrder("anu", "SKU-9", 2, 998.0);
class OrderFacade(
    private val inventory: Inventory, private val payment: Payment,
    private val shipping: Shipping, private val notifier: Notifier,
) {
    fun placeOrder(user: String, sku: String, qty: Int, amount: Double) {
        inventory.reserve(sku, qty)
        runCatching { payment.charge(user, amount) }
            .onFailure { inventory.release(sku, qty); throw it }
        shipping.create(user, sku)
        notifier.send(user, "Order placed")
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the failure path (compensation) which is the real value of the facade.
  • Hiding the subsystem entirely so power users cannot reach it.

notes.title: Facade: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when the subsystem is already one simple class; wrapping it adds a pointless layer. Do not use it to hide a bad design you could fix.

Avoid it if it grows to 40 methods: that is a god object; split by use case (OrderFacade, RefundFacade).

Distributed variant: a facade across microservices (an API gateway or BFF, backend-for-frontend) adds latency (+1 hop, often 1 to 5 ms) and becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure unless replicated.

Worked example. A AppFacade with 60 methods meant every release touched it and merge conflicts hit weekly. Splitting into 5 focused facades cut conflicts to rare.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any service class a facade. A facade specifically simplifies a complex subsystem.
  • Not thinking about transactions when the facade crosses services.

notes.title: Flyweight: the idea
notes.html:
Flyweight saves memory by sharing the common, unchanging part of many similar objects. Split object state into intrinsic (shared, immutable, stored in the flyweight) and extrinsic (varies per use, passed in by the caller).

Mechanism: a factory keeps a pool (map). When asked for a flyweight with a given intrinsic key, it returns the existing one or creates it once.

 Context objects (millions)           Flyweight pool (few)
+-------------------------+          +----------------------+
| Tree: x=10, y=7, kind --+--------->| TreeType "Oak"       |
| Tree: x=44, y=2, kind --+--------->|  texture (2 MB)      |
| Tree: x=91, y=30,kind --+--------->|  mesh                |
+-------------------------+          +----------------------+
 extrinsic: x, y                      intrinsic: texture, mesh

Worked example. A game draws 1,000,000 trees of 5 species. A texture and mesh is 2 MB. Naively: 1,000,000 x 2 MB = 2 TB (impossible). With Flyweight: 5 x 2 MB = 10 MB shared, plus 1,000,000 x 16 bytes (x, y, type reference) = 16 MB. About 26 MB total.

Industry examples. Integer.valueOf(n) caches -128 to 127; so Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b is true but with 1000 it is false. String interning (the string pool). Android Glide and Fresco bitmap pools, Pools.SimplePool and RecyclerView's shared RecycledViewPool (reuse of view holders). Text editors share one glyph object per character.

Everyday analogy. A print shop keeps one metal stamp per letter and presses it at different positions, instead of carving a new stamp for every letter on the page.

Decision gravity. An optimization: reversible but invasive, because you split state into intrinsic and extrinsic everywhere. Do it only after measuring memory. It trades memory for a little CPU and API awkwardness.

Common interview traps.

  • Flyweight objects MUST be immutable (or at least their intrinsic part); otherwise one change corrupts all users.
  • Using == on boxed Integers is a classic bug that stems from the flyweight cache.

notes.title: Flyweight in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before.

// BEFORE: each Tree owns its own 2 MB texture copy
class Tree {
    final byte[] texture = loadTexture("oak.png"); // 2 MB each
    int x, y;
}

After.

import java.util.*;

final class TreeType {                    // flyweight: immutable, shared
    final String name; final byte[] texture;
    TreeType(String name) { this.name = name; this.texture = new byte[2 * 1024 * 1024]; }
}

final class TreeTypeFactory {
    private static final Map<String, TreeType> POOL = new HashMap<>();
    static TreeType get(String name) {
        return POOL.computeIfAbsent(name, TreeType::new);   // not thread-safe pool = see note
    }
}

class Tree {                              // context: only extrinsic state
    final int x, y; final TreeType type;
    Tree(int x, int y, TreeType type) { this.x = x; this.y = y; this.type = type; }
}

// new Tree(10, 7, TreeTypeFactory.get("Oak"))  -> same TreeType for all oaks
class TreeType(val name: String) { val texture = ByteArray(2 * 1024 * 1024) }

object TreeTypeFactory {
    private val pool = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, TreeType>()
    fun get(name: String) = pool.computeIfAbsent(name) { TreeType(it) }
}

class Tree(val x: Int, val y: Int, val type: TreeType)

Thread safety. A plain HashMap pool breaks under concurrent access; use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (Kotlin version above). Also the pool can leak if keys are unbounded; consider WeakReference values or an LRU.

Common interview traps.

  • Sharing mutable state in the "flyweight".
  • Forgetting the factory; without it nothing is shared.
  • Not stating the numbers (2 TB vs 26 MB) that justify the pattern.

notes.title: Flyweight: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when there are few objects (a thousand small objects cost kilobytes) or when little state is shareable. The pattern then only adds complexity.

Do not use it when objects are mutable per instance or when extrinsic state is costly to compute or pass on every call (CPU cost beats memory savings).

On modern JVMs and Android, premature pooling can hurt: young-generation GC is cheap, and object pools add contention, stale state bugs and memory that never gets freed. Pool large or expensive things (bitmaps, DB connections), not small ones.

Worked example. A team pooled 24-byte Point objects. The pool lock added about 40 ns per access, more than the allocation it saved (about 10 ns), and the heap dropped by 0 MB. They removed it.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Flyweight always speeds things up. It saves memory, often at CPU cost.
  • Confusing it with caching: caching avoids recomputation; Flyweight shares identical immutable objects.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Facade: a simple front door over a complex subsystem; put orchestration and compensation in one place; keep the subsystem accessible; do not grow a god facade. Examples: MediaPlayer, JdbcTemplate, Stripe PaymentIntent, BFF/API gateway.
  • Facade simplifies many classes; Adapter converts one interface.
  • Flyweight: share immutable intrinsic state through a factory; pass extrinsic state in. Example numbers: 2 TB down to 26 MB. Examples: Integer.valueOf cache, string pool, Glide bitmap pool, RecycledViewPool.
  • Make flyweights immutable and thread-safe; avoid pooling small objects on modern GCs.
  • Use Flyweight only after measuring; use Facade when callers repeat the same multi-step recipe.
